title: From data to a DBMS
lead: Start with two books and one loan: can the library answer which physical copy is available?
goals: Distinguish a database, a DBMS, a schema, and an instance
Explain the three levels of abstraction through an example
Identify the system responsibilities behind a query

sections.title: What must a library remember?
sections.html:
A visitor asks: “Is book B17 available?” A list of titles cannot answer. We also need to know which physical copy is on loan. Start with these original teaching rows:

Book(book_id, title)          Loan(book_id, member_id)
B17  Databases               B17  M3
B18  Networks

Read B17 in Book: the copy exists. Then find B17 in Loan: member M3 has borrowed it. Our answer is “not available”. B18 exists and has no Loan row, so it is available under this simple model. We assume every Loan row is an open loan and each book_id identifies one physical copy.

The related facts form a database. The software that stores them, answers questions and coordinates updates is a database management system (DBMS). A database is the data; a DBMS manages it. Neither term means just the screen used by the librarian.

Notice three different choices. Using tables with named columns is a data model, here the relational model. Choosing Book(book_id,title) and Loan(book_id,member_id) is a schema: the structure of this library. The two Book rows and one Loan row are its current instance. A column is also called an attribute; a row is also called a tuple. A shop can use the same model with Product and Order tables. Graph models instead describe vertices and edges; document models describe documents and fields.

Try: the librarian enters B19, “Compilers”. Which of model, schema and instance changes?

The instance changes: another row now fits the existing Book structure. Adding a publication_year column would change the schema. Neither requires abandoning the relational model.

Do a library and a shop necessarily need different data models?

No. Both can use the relational model with different schemas and instances.

sections.title: A valid file can still describe an impossible library
sections.html:
Now rename B17 to B017. Both the book and its loan must refer to the same copy afterward. Here is what happens if two independent file writes are interrupted:

MomentBook IDsLoan book_idCan the loan find its book?
BeforeB17, B18B17Yes
After writing books.csvB017, B18B17No
After writing loans.csvB017, B18B017Yes

A crash after the middle row leaves two perfectly readable files but a broken relationship. A constraint expresses the rule “every loan refers to an existing book”. A transaction groups the two changes into one unit; atomicity means the finished database must contain both changes or neither. Changing CSV to JSON does not remove this interruption point.

A second failure needs a different explanation. Mai and Nam both read a Loan file containing one row. Mai adds loan L2 and writes two rows. Nam adds L3 to his older copy and writes it: L2 disappears. Each writer finished, so all-or-nothing updates alone do not explain the lost update. We need coordination between simultaneous users. Later transaction lectures develop the mechanisms; for now identify the failure each mechanism must prevent.

File programs also repeat work: each new question needs parsing and searching code; repeated facts can disagree; borrower records should not be visible to every catalogue user. A DBMS supplies query processing, constraints, coordinated updates and access privileges. An index, introduced later, can help locate a key. These facilities still need correct schema and application design.

Try: two people lend the same physical copy after both see it as available. Which rule must be protected?

At most one open loan may exist for each physical copy. Checking availability twice is insufficient if both checks happen before either write. The check and change must be coordinated as transactions.

Key takeaway

Changing the file format does not fix update errors. Both CSV and JSON can contain broken references or suffer overwritten changes. The system needs constraint checking, all-or-nothing updates, and coordinated writes.

Does converting the files to JSON prevent the partial identifier update?

No. Format does not coordinate writes; constraints and an atomic update procedure are needed.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 13–17. Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: Change the storage without changing the question
sections.html:
Imagine moving the Book rows to a new file layout. The visitor still asks whether B17 is available. If every catalogue screen must change because a row moved by 100 bytes, application meaning is tied too tightly to storage.

We separate three descriptions of this same library:

LevelLibrary decisionWhat a change means
ViewVisitor sees title and availability; librarian sees borrowerExpose a different relevant subset
LogicalBook and Loan tables connected by book_idChange the structure or relationships
PhysicalPlace bytes in files and use an index to locate themChange how data is represented and reached

This is abstraction: each description hides details its user does not need. Physical data independence means a storage change can leave the logical questions intact. Changing a page size from 4 KiB to 8 KiB should not alter which loans exist. A page is a chunk managed in reads and writes; you do not need to choose its layout to write the library question.

Independence has limits. Deleting the borrower column changes the logical information available, so a view showing borrower names cannot keep working unchanged. Conversely, adding one Book row changes the instance, not any of these structural definitions.

Try: add borrower email, hide it from visitors, then move its bytes. Classify each decision.

Adding email changes the logical schema. Choosing who sees it is a view/access decision. Moving its byte location is physical. One feature can require all three decisions; they answer different questions.

Key takeaway

A schema describes structure; an instance is the current data. Distinguishing these changes helps you decide whether an application needs another data row or a new structure for representing its data.

Does adding a book change the schema?

Adding a row changes the instance. Adding a new column changes the schema.

Current explanation scope: official PDF physical pages 18–19. Numerical fixtures are original teaching examples.

sections.title: Keep the question; learn the machinery when it is needed
sections.html:
Before studying the internals, make an answer you can check. On our three original rows, “which copies are available?” returns B18 only. Every later algorithm must preserve that answer. Being faster is useless if it invents a second copy or loses the open loan.

There are three useful steps behind a request. First, understand the question and choose operations that compute it; this is query planning. Second, perform those operations on rows; this is execution. Third, obtain the stored data those operations need. File/index management locates records, buffer management holds pages in RAM, and disk-space management reads or writes their stored bytes. You will trace those responsibilities in Lecture 4 and Lecture 5; there is no need to memorise the whole architecture now. Concurrency control coordinates overlapping operations, and recovery handles failures across the layers.

The question also determines the workload. One visitor's availability lookup is short transactional work, commonly called OLTP. Counting all loans by month is analytical work, commonly called OLAP. A hybrid system, HTAP, serves both. These labels describe work, while “disk-oriented” and “in-memory” describe storage architecture. A disk-oriented system can cache pages in RAM; a RAM write alone still disappears on power loss. Row and column layouts arrange fields differently and are developed in Lecture 7, where their costs become visible.

The official introduction also gives the Spring 2026 course roadmap, prerequisites, assessment and academic-integrity guidance. Those historical dates are not current deadlines. This site supplies original practice rather than access to assessed Learn worksheets.

Before SQL: write the expected answer if Loan becomes empty.

Both B17 and B18 become available under our stated open-loan model. A changed algorithm must return this new answer too; testing one fixed instance is only the start.

Does a cache hit make a disk-oriented database an in-memory architecture?

No. It avoids that read, but does not redefine the database architecture or make a RAM write durable.

quiz.question: Changing a record’s byte position primarily belongs to which level?
quiz.explanation: A byte position is a physical representation detail; the schema describes the meaning and structure of the data.
